text: {"decision":"GO","artifact":{"author":"Graham Hill","audience":"Business and IT leaders","format":"Independent editorial draft","title":"Valid access is not proof of a legitimate action","body":[{"type":"reported_fact","text":"Cloudflare reports that one service token and three accounts stolen in the October 2023 Okta compromise were left unrotated because they were mistakenly considered unused. Attackers subsequently used those credentials to access its Atlassian environment. A credential can still work after the reason to trust its holder has disappeared. [CF2024]"},{"type":"term_analysis","text":"The consequential term is ‘valid credentials’, explicit in CERT-In’s October advisory and operationally illustrated by Cloudflare’s account. These sources do not supply a shared formal definition or a numerical measure of credential validity. Their incident descriptions establish acceptance: credentials enabled access or API invocation. Acceptance does not establish that the actor or the particular action was authorized. [CF2024; CIAD-2026-0046]"},{"type":"reported_fact","text":"CERT-In reports attackers invoking fund-transfer APIs with valid credentials from victims’ own whitelisted infrastructure, bypassing application checks such as sanction and beneficiary verification. Its November update describes another weakness in origin-based trust: requests arriving through shared, whitelisted third-party fetcher pools that Internet users could cause to fetch arbitrary URLs. These are distinct mechanisms for making an attacker’s request arrive through an accepted route. [CIAD-2026-0046; CIAD-2026-0058]"},{"type":"inference","text":"Two readings of ‘valid’ lead to different decisions. Under an acceptance reading, a working credential and an approved source address can be treated as sufficient grounds to proceed. Under an authorization reading, they establish only part of the case: the system must also establish permission for this action and evidence that its required business checks occurred. The reported attacks expose the gap between those readings."},{"type":"hypothetical_illustration","text":"Consider a hypothetical payout request with an accepted API key and an approved source IP, but no corresponding sanctioned record. A rule that treats accepted access as sufficient would release it. A rule requiring evidence of transaction authorization would reject or hold it. This illustrates the decision difference; it is not an additional reported incident."},{"type":"evidence_assessment","text":"The evidence is incident-based, not a controlled comparison. Cloudflare describes credential handling and the resulting access retrospectively. CERT-In describes patterns from reported incidents, including dummy references without corresponding records and bypassed transaction checks. The supplied material provides no common denominator, false-acceptance rate or measured effectiveness for its recommendations. The November advisory updates the October reporting chain; it is not independent replication. [CF2024; CIAD-2026-0046; CIAD-2026-0058]"},{"type":"ambiguity_vs_conflict","text":"The ambiguity is linguistic: ‘valid’ can mean technically accepted or legitimately authorized. The reported outcomes do not establish a factual conflict. Cloudflare says segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement, with no customer data or global network changes affected. CERT-In describes unauthorized transfers in different organizations and systems. Controls limiting one incident can coexist with attackers bypassing different controls elsewhere. Neither finding demonstrates universal success or failure. [CF2024; CIAD-2026-0046]"},{"type":"inference","text":"Previously trusted access stops being sufficient evidence of legitimate action when credentials can be used by an unauthorized holder, an approved origin can relay an outsider’s request, or a sensitive API can run without proof of preceding authorization checks. Detection may come later than that loss of evidential value. For leaders, the useful review question is concrete: what evidence authorizes this transaction beyond the fact that the request got through?"}]},"claim_support":[{"claim":"Stolen credentials left unrotated enabled later access to Cloudflare’s Atlassian environment.","source_ids":["CF2024"],"locator":"Opening and October18 timeline","status":"Reported fact in supplied victim account"},{"claim":"Attackers invoked payment APIs using valid credentials from whitelisted victim infrastructure and bypassed application controls.","source_ids":["CIAD-2026-0046"],"locator":"Description; URLs and underlying incident evidence were not independently verified.","The Cloudflare material consists of selected passages and supplied claim summaries, while the CERT-In material contains advisory text.","‘Valid credentials’ is explicit in CERT-In and conceptually illustrated by Cloudflare; a common verbatim definition across sources is not established.","The comparison concerns a shared trust mechanism across different organizations, periods and systems. It does not establish a shared attacker or comparable incident severity.","No supplied common measurement method supports a numerical estimate of when trust fails or how reliably a proposed control prevents abuse.","The hypothetical payout is explicitly illustrative. Recommendations and editorial inferences are distinguished from reported outcomes."]}
